    Solutions to Weinberg Exercises
    These editorial solutions were added by Codex and are not part of Weinberg’s original text.

W.15.1. In any representation,

                           [Dµ , [Dν , Dλ ]] + [Dν , [Dλ , Dµ ]] + [Dλ , [Dµ , Dν ]] = 0

          by the Jacobi identity for operator commutators. Using [Dν , Dλ ] = −itα Fανλ and
          letting the outer derivative act on an arbitrary matter field gives
                                                                 
                                    −itα Dµ Fανλ Dν Fαλµ Dλ Fαµν = 0.

          Here the derivative on the field strength is the adjoint covariant derivative,

                                      Dµ Fανλ = ∂µ Fανλ Cαβγ Aβµ Fγνλ .

          Faithfulness is not needed: the same identity follows componentwise by inserting the
          definition of F and using the Jacobi identity for Cαβγ . This proves the stated Bianchi
          identity.

W.15.2. An infinitesimal gauge transformation gives

                            δfα = ∂i (Di λ)α ,      (Di λ)α = ∂i λα + Cαγβ Aγi λβ .

          Thus the Faddeev–Popov operator and ghost action are
                                                           Z
                               x   x      4
                     Fαx,βy = ∂i (Di )αβ δ (x − y), IGH = d4 x ωα∗ ∂i (Di ω)α .




                                                  – 58 –
          After a spatial integration by parts,

                                 LGH = −∂i ωα∗ ∂i ωα + Cαβγ (∂i ωα∗ )Aγi ωβ ,

          where antisymmetry of the structure constants has been used in the interaction term.
          The field-independent kernel is δαβ ∇2 . In the propagator convention of Eq. (15.6.12),
          its inverse is
                                                             d3 p −eip·(x−y)
                                                         Z
                                                  0    0
                            ∆αβ (x, y) = δαβ δ(x − y )                       .
                                                            (2π)3     p2
          Equivalently its momentum kernel is −δαβ /p2 . The overall sign is reversed if −∇2 ,
          rather than ∇2 , is used as the positive spatial operator. The important feature is the
          absence of a p0 pole: Coulomb-gauge ghosts propagate instantaneously.

W.15.3. In electrodynamics δAµ = ∂µ λ, so

                                           δf = (□ + 2cAµ ∂µ ) λ.

          The ghost Lagrangian therefore is

                         LGH = ω ∗ (□ + 2cAµ ∂µ ) ω = −∂µ ω ∗ ∂ µ ω + 2c ω ∗ Aµ ∂µ ω,

          up to a surface term in the second form. Its free kernel is still □, and hence

                                                         d4 p eip·(x−y)
                                                    Z
                                       ∆(x, y) =                        .
                                                        (2π)4 p2 − iϵ

          Unlike ghosts in a linear Abelian gauge, these ghosts do not decouple: the nonlinear
          term in f produces a photon–ghost–antighost vertex.

W.15.4. For the compact Lie algebras relevant here, complexify the algebra and choose a
        Cartan subalgebra of rank r. Its root decomposition gives

                                             dim g = r + 2N+ ,

          where N+ is the number of positive roots. If dim g = 4, then r is even. The possibility
          r = 4 has no roots and is Abelian, hence is not simple. The only remaining possibility
          is r = 2 and N+ = 1. But then the roots are only ±α, and they span a one-dimensional
          subspace of the two-dimensional dual Cartan algebra. A nonzero Cartan element H
          annihilated by α commutes both with the Cartan subalgebra and with the two root
          spaces. It is therefore central, again contradicting simplicity. Thus no compact simple
          Lie algebra has four generators.

W.15.5. Write Aµ = tα Aαµ . Successive transport along the sides of an infinitesimal parallelo-
        gram with side vectors aµ and bµ gives, through second order,

                                 ψfinal − ψinitial = i tα Fαµν (X)aµ bν ψ(X).




                                                  – 59 –
         For a general small loop the oriented area bivector is
                                        I                       I
                                      1
                                µν
                               Σ =        (x dx − x dx ) = xµ dxν .
                                            µ   ν     ν   µ
                                      2 γ                        γ

         Consequently                                   I
                            δγ ψ = i tα Fαµν (X)ψ(X)         xµ dxν + O(area3/2 ),
                                                        γ

         and the requested proportionality constant is i.
         Now suppose Fµν = 0 in a simply connected finite region R. Parallel transport from
         a fixed point x0 to x is path independent there: two paths differ by a closed loop,
         and the latter can be tiled by small loops with trivial holonomy. Let U (x, x0 ) be this
         transport matrix. It obeys

                                        (∂µ − iAµ )U (x, x0 ) = 0.

         The finite gauge transformation by U −1 therefore changes the connection to A′µ = 0
         throughout R. The qualification about the region is essential: a flat connection can
         have nontrivial holonomy on a multiply connected space.

W.15.6. The quadratic gauge-field kernel in momentum space is

                                    Kµν = p2 ηµν − pµ pν + ξ −1 nµ nν .

         Direct multiplication shows that its inverse is

                                                                  n2 + ξp2
                                                                                
                                    δαβ           pµ nν + nµ pν
                     ∆αµ,βν (p) = 2         ηµν −               +           pµ pν .
                                   p − iϵ              p·n         (p · n)2

         As usual in an axial gauge, the factors 1/(p · n) require a specified pole prescription.
         In the sharp-gauge limit ξ → 0, the propagator is transverse to nµ .
         The gauge variation of fα = nµ Aαµ is

                                            δfα = nµ (Dµ λ)α ,

         and hence
                        LGH = ωα∗ nµ (Dµ ω)α = ωα∗ nµ ∂µ ωα + Cαγβ ωα∗ nµ Aγµ ωβ .
         The free ghost propagator is the inverse of n · ∂:
                                                             δαβ
                                            ∆αβ (p) =
                                                            in · p
         with a compatible prescription. With all momenta incoming, the ghost–antighost–
         gauge vertex is proportional to Cαγβ nµ (and acquires the conventional factor i when
         the usual iLint Feynman rule is used). In the strict axial gauge n · A = 0, this
         interaction vanishes on the gauge slice; the determinant reduces to det(n · ∂), so the
         ghosts decouple.

W.15.7. Assign dimensions
                                   [Aµ ] = [ω] = [ω ∗ ] = 1,    [h] = 2,
         and ghost numbers 0, 1, −1, 0, respectively. The cohomology argument of Section 15.8
         says that every local BRST-invariant action of ghost number zero has the form

                                             I = I0 [A] + sΨ,

         where I0 is gauge invariant and Ψ is a Lorentz- and global-gauge-invariant fermion of
         ghost number −1.
         For a semisimple gauge algebra, the gauge-field part of the most general density of
         dimension at most four is, up to a constant, a surface term, and independent invariant
         quadratic forms on simple factors,
                                       1               1
                                 L0 = − Zαβ Fαµν Fβµν + ϑαβ Fαµν Feβµν .
                                       4               4
         (For Abelian factors one may add the familiar gauge-invariant terms permitted by
         their invariant tensors.) Modulo integrations by parts, the most general renormaliz-
         able gauge-fixing fermion density is
                                                  1
                             ψ = zαβ ωα∗ ∂µ Aµβ + ξαβ ωα∗ hβ + aαβγ ωα∗ Aµβ Aγµ
                                                  2
                                    1         ∗ ∗
                                 + bαβγ ωα ωβ ωγ ,
                                    4
         where all coefficient tensors are invariant under the global gauge group, aαβγ = aαγβ ,
         and bαβγ = −bβαγ . Thus the answer is

                                               L = L0 + sψ

         up to total derivatives and field-independent constants. The usual linear covari-
         ant gauge is obtained with zαβ ∝ δαβ , ξαβ ∝ δαβ , and a = b = 0. The last two
         terms display interactions allowed by the stated principles but absent in that spe-
         cial Faddeev–Popov choice, including, after applying s, nonlinear gauge-fixing and
         four-ghost interactions.

W.15.8. Let ϵF denote the Grassmann parity of F . Moving a functional derivative through
        a homogeneous functional and exchanging left and right derivatives in Eq. (15.9.13)
        gives
                               (F, G) = −(−1)(ϵF +1)(ϵG +1) (G, F ).
         If F and G are both bosonic the sign is +; in every other case it is −, precisely
         Eq. (15.9.15).
         For the Jacobi identity, collect fields and antifields into coordinates z A = (χn , χ‡n ).
         The bracket can be written
                                                    ←
                                                    −        →
                                                             −
                                                     δ        δG
                                       (F, G) = F A E AB B ,
                                                   δz        δz



                                               – 61 –
         where E AB is the constant odd symplectic matrix with only field–antifield blocks
         nonzero. Expanding (F, (G, H)), the terms containing one second derivative cancel in
         the graded cyclic sum because E AB has graded antisymmetry; the terms containing
         a second derivative of G or H cancel in the same way. Hence
                        (−1)(ϵF +1)(ϵH +1) (F, (G, H)) + cyclic permutations = 0.
         Its first coefficient is −1 only when F and H are both bosonic, and is +1 otherwise,
         which is the sign convention of Eq. (15.9.21).

W.15.9. There is a necessary editorial correction in the stated condition. The quantum-
        observable condition is
                          (O, S) = i∆O,       or       σO ≡ (O, S) − i∆O = 0,
         as also stated in the footnote following Eq. (15.9.36). The printed right-hand side
         i∆S does not imply gauge-fixing independence for a general O.
         To prove the corrected statement, vary the gauge fermion by δΨ, so the Lagrangian
         submanifold χ‡n = δΨ/δχn is shifted anticanonically. Field-space integration by parts,
         including the Jacobian measured by ∆, gives the normalized variation
                                 δΨ ⟨O⟩ = i σ(O δΨ) − i⟨O⟩ σ(δΨ) .
         BV integration by parts makes the expectation value of every σ-exact insertion vanish
         when
                                         1
                                           (S, S) − i∆S = 0.
                                         2
         Moreover, the quantum master equation implies σ 2 = 0, and the graded product rule
         reduces the remaining term to one proportional to σO. It therefore vanishes for a
         quantum observable:
                                             δΨ ⟨O⟩ = 0.
         When O depends only on the fields, ∆O = 0, so the condition reduces to ordinary
         generalized BRST invariance (O, S) = 0, in agreement with Eq. (15.9.36).

 S.15.1. Curvature from Parallel Transport

         (a) Acting on a test field,

                               [Dµ , Dν ]ψ = −i (∂µ Aν − ∂ν Aµ − i[Aµ , Aν ]) ψ.

             Thus
                                       Fµν = ∂µ Aν − ∂ν Aµ − i[Aµ , Aν ],
             which in components is Eq. (15.1.13). A finite gauge transformation is defined
             by requiring Dµ′ ψ ′ = U Dµ ψ with ψ ′ = U ψ; hence Dµ′ = U Dµ U −1 . It follows
             without further expansion that

                                [Dµ′ , Dν′ ] = U [Dµ , Dν ]U −1 = −iU Fµν U −1 .

             Comparing this with [Dµ′ , Dν′ ] = −iFµν
                                                   ′ gives F ′ = U F U −1 .
                                                            µν      µν




                                               – 68 –
       (b) The transporter on a short displacement uµ from z is
                                            i                 1
             U (z + u, z) = 1 + iuµ Aµ (z) + uµ uν ∂µ Aν (z) − uµ uν Aµ (z)Aν (z) + O(u3 ).
                                            2                 2
           Multiply the corresponding expressions for the four oriented sides in their
           traversal order. The terms linear in a or b cancel. The derivative terms give
           i(∂µ Aν − ∂ν Aµ )aµ bν , while the products whose order differs on the two routes
           give [Aµ , Aν ]aµ bν . Therefore

             U□ = 1 + i ∂µ Aν − ∂ν Aµ − i[Aµ , Aν ] aµ bν + O(ℓ3 ) = 1 + iFµν aµ bν + O(ℓ3 ).
                                                   


           Replacing the ordered product by an ordinary exponential would symmetrize the
           matrix factors and lose the commutator; path ordering is precisely what retains
           the non-Abelian part of the curvature.

S.15.2. Yang–Mills Equation and Covariant Conservation

       (a) Applying a covariant divergence to the field equation gives
                                                      1
                                 Dν J ν = Dν Dµ F µν = [Dν , Dµ ]F µν .
                                                      2
           In the adjoint representation, [Dν , Dµ ]X = −i[Fνµ , X], up to the convention for
           where g is absorbed. Therefore
                                                 i
                                       Dν J ν = − [Fνµ , F µν ] = 0.
                                                 2
           The last contraction vanishes because interchanging the two field strengths re-
           verses the Lie bracket while leaving the summed Lorentz indices unchanged.
           Thus the Yang–Mills equation requires the covariant, rather than ordinary, con-
           servation law
                                             Dν J ν = 0.
                                  ′
       (b) Since Ψ′ = U Ψ and Ψ = ΨU −1 ,

                                 J ′ν = gΨU −1 γ ν T a U Ψ T a = U J ν U −1 ,

           where the final equality is the matrix form of the adjoint action on the compo-
           nents.
           The transformed covariant derivative satisfies Dµ′ = U Dµ U −1 , while F ′µν =
           U F µν U −1 . Acting on the curvature therefore gives

                                       Dµ′ F ′µν = U (Dµ F µν )U −1 .

           Both sides of the field equation transform homogeneously in the adjoint repre-
           sentation, so its covariance follows from the independent transformations of the
           matter current and curvature.

S.15.3. Equal Curvature Is Not Gauge Equivalence

       (a) If Abelian connections A and A′ have the same curvature, then d(A′ − A) = 0.
           The Poincaré lemma on a contractible patch gives A′ −A = dλ, which is precisely
           a local Abelian gauge transformation. The corresponding non-Abelian equation
           contains a commutator and does not reduce to the statement that the difference
           is a closed one-form.
       (b) Since the first connection is proportional to T3 , its components commute. There-
           fore                            gx          gy 
                                Fxy = ∂x       T3 − ∂y − T3 = gT3 .
                                             2                2
           For the constant second connection the derivative terms vanish, while
                                    ′
                                   Fxy = −ig[T1 , T2 ] = −ig(iT3 ) = gT3 .

           Thus the two curvatures agree pointwise.
        (c) The covariant derivative of the curvature transforms by conjugation. For the
            first connection it vanishes,

                                           Dx Fxy = Dy Fxy = 0,

           because both Aµ and Fxy lie in the T3 direction. For the second connection,

                  Dx′ Fxy
                       ′
                          = −ig[T1 , gT3 ] = −g 2 T2 ,    Dy′ Fxy
                                                               ′
                                                                  = −ig[T2 , gT3 ] = g 2 T1 .

           With tr(Ta Tb ) = δab /2, the local gauge-invariant scalar

                                      I = tr (Dx Fxy )2 + (Dy Fxy )2
                                                                    

           is zero for the first connection and g 4 for the second. Gauge transformations
           cannot change a conjugation-invariant scalar, so one such mismatch is enough
           to rule out gauge equivalence.

S.15.9. Lie-Algebra BRST Cohomology

       (a) Decompose Q = ρ + dCE , where ρ = ω a Ra acts on the representation factor
           and dCE ω a = − 12 C a bc ω b ω c . For a constant representation vector v, the graded
           Leibniz rule gives
                                          1
                                  Q2 v = − C c ab ω a ω b Rc v − ω a ω b Rb Ra v.
                                          2
           Anticommutativity retains only the commutator in the second term:
                                              1                    1
                              −ω a ω b Rb Ra = ω a ω b [Ra , Rb ] = C c ab ω a ω b Rc ,
                                              2                    2
           so the representation-dependent terms cancel. On a ghost generator,
                                              1
                                      Q2 ω a = C a e[b C e cd] ω b ω c ω d = 0,
                                              6
           by the Jacobi identity. Since Q is an odd derivation, it therefore squares to zero
           on every R-valued polynomial.
       (b) In the trivial representation, the polynomial algebra is Λ• g∗ , and Q is the
           Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. Applying it to the three-cochain produces four
           ghosts:
                                     1
                             QΩ = − Cabc C a de ω d ω e ω b ω c + cyclic terms.
                                     12
           After total antisymmetrization, its coefficient is the invariant-metric form of the
           Jacobi identity,
                                            Ca[bc C a de] = 0,
           so QΩ = 0.
           This is the Cartan three-cocycle and represents the nonzero generator of H 3 (g)
           for each compact simple factor. For su(2), choose Cabc = ϵabc . Then Ω = ω 1 ω 2 ω 3 ,
           apart from normalization, and

                            Qω 1 = −ω 2 ω 3 ,    Qω 2 = −ω 3 ω 1 ,     Qω 3 = −ω 1 ω 2 .

           Every quadratic monomial has zero Q-image because a ghost is repeated. There-
           fore no degree-two polynomial can map to Ω, proving non-exactness explicitly.
           Restriction to the SU (2) subgroup associated with a root gives the same ob-
           struction in the general compact simple case.

    Exchange F and G in the defining expression. Moving the two derivatives and

    If E AB = E AB (z), the surviving coefficient is the graded cyclic sum of

                                         E AD ∂D E BC .

                                        – 82 –
16     External Field Methods

It is often useful to consider quantum field theories in the presence of a classical exter-
nal field. One reason is that in many physical situations, there really is an external field
present, such as a classical electromagnetic or gravitational field, or a scalar field with a
non-vanishing vacuum expectation value. (As we shall see in Chapter 19, such scalar fields
can play an important role in the spontaneous breakdown of symmetries of the Lagrangian.)
But even where there is no actual external field present in a problem, some calculations are
greatly facilitated by considering physical amplitudes in the presence of a fictitious external
field. This chapter will show that it is possible to take all multiloop effects into account by
summing ‘tree’ graphs whose vertices and propagators are taken from a quantum effective
action, which is nothing but the one-particle-irreducible connected vacuum–vacuum am-
plitude in the presence of an external field. It will turn out in the next chapter that this
provides an especially handy way both of completing the proof of the renormalizability of
non-Abelian gauge theories begun in Chapter 15, and of calculating the charge renormal-
ization factors that we need in order to establish the crucial property of asymptotic freedom
in quantum chromodynamics.

16.1    The Quantum Effective Action
Consider a quantum field theory with action I[ϕ], and suppose we ‘turn on’ a set of classical
currents Jr (x) coupled to the fields ϕr (x) of the theory. The complete vacuum vacuum
amplitude in the presence of these currents is then

We sometimes work with functionals Z[J] defined by (16.1.1) where the ϕr (x) are not

     Now, Z[J] is given by the sum of all vacuum–vacuum amplitudes in the presence of

different those diagrams that differ only by a permutation of vertices in the same or different
connected subdiagrams. A general diagram that consists of N connected components will
contribute to Z[J] a term equal to the product of the contributions of these components,
divided by the number N ! of permutations of vertices that merely permute all the vertices
in one connected component with all the vertices in another.22 Hence, the sum of all graphs

and E. Weinberg [3] in a study of spontaneous symmetry breaking, the subject of Chapters
19 and 21. The results were also used by them in one of the early applications of the
renormalization group, to be described in Section 18.2.

sign is opposite because (as shown in Chapter 9) fermionic path integrals of Gaussians
give a result proportional to the determinant of the matrix coefficient in the exponent,
while bosonic path integrals of Gaussians give a result proportional to the inverse of this
determinant.

16.3   Energy Interpretation
The effective action Γ[ϕ] and potential V [ϕ] have an important interpretation in terms of
the energy and energy density respectively [4]. To see this, suppose that we turn on a




                                            – 90 –
current J n (x, t) that rises smoothly from zero at t = −∞ to a finite value J n (x), and
remains at that value for a long time T , after which it drops smoothly again to zero at
t = +∞. The effect of this perturbation is to convert the vacuum to a state with a definite
energy E[J ] (a functional of J n (x)), in which it remains for a time T , after which it returns
to the vacuum. However, although the ‘out’ vacuum is the same physical state as the ‘in’
vacuum, the state vectors differ by the phase exp(−iE[J ]T ) accumulated during the time
T:
                                                              
                                out⟨Ω|Ω⟩in,J = exp −iE[J ]T .                            (16.3.1)

Comparing with Eqs. (16.1.1) and (16.1.3), this gives

                                       W [J] = −E[J ]T.                                 (16.3.2)

    To see the connection between this energy and the effective action, suppose we seek
the state |Ωϕ ⟩ that minimizes the energy expectation value

                                                 ⟨Ω|H|Ω⟩
                                      ⟨H⟩Ω =             ,                              (16.3.3)
                                                  ⟨Ω|Ω⟩

subject to the condition that the quantum fields Φn (x, t) have the time-independent expec-
tation value ϕn (x)
                                  ⟨Ω|Φn (x, t)|Ω⟩
                                                  = ϕn (x).                        (16.3.4)
                                      ⟨Ω|Ω⟩
It is convenient also to impose the condition that |Ω⟩ is normalized

                                          ⟨Ω|Ω⟩ = 1.                                    (16.3.5)

To minimize the expectation value (16.3.3) subject to the constraints (16.3.4) and (16.3.5),
we use the method of Lagrange multipliers, and instead minimize the quantity
                                           Z
                     ⟨Ω|H|Ω⟩ − α⟨Ω|Ω⟩ − d3 x β n (x)⟨Ω|Φn (x)|Ω⟩                    (16.3.6)

with no constraints on |Ω⟩. This gives
                                             Z
                            H|Ω⟩ = α|Ω⟩ +        d3 x β n (x)Φn (x)|Ω⟩.                 (16.3.7)

Both α and β n (x) are to be chosen in such a way as to satisfy the constraints (16.3.4) and
(16.3.5) and therefore depend functionally on the prescribed expectation value ϕn (x).
    Now, we have said that in the presence of a current J n (x), the Hamiltonian H −
R 3
  d x J n (x)Φn (x) has an eigenvalue E[J ]:
                             Z                 
                                 3    n
                         H − d x J (x)Φn (x) |ΨJ ⟩ = E[J ]|ΨJ ⟩                      (16.3.8)

with a normalized eigenvector |ΨJ ⟩. Furthermore, since slowly turning on this current
converts the vacuum into this energy eigenstate, we can presume that E[J ] is the lowest




                                             – 91 –
energy eigenstate in the presence of this current. Therefore Eqs. (16.3.4), (16.3.5), and
(16.3.7) are satisfied by

                                 |Ω⟩ = |ΨJϕ ⟩,                                        (16.3.9)
                                  α = E[Jϕ ],                                       (16.3.10)
                             n
                         β       (x) = Jϕn (x),                                     (16.3.11)

where Jϕ (x) is the current for which Φ(x) has an expectation value ϕ(x) in the state |ΨJ ⟩.
    Setting J = Jϕ in Eq. (16.3.8) and taking the scalar product with |ΨJϕ ⟩, the minimum
energy of states in which the fields Φn are constrained to have the expectation values ϕn is
seen to be                                   Z
                            ⟨H⟩Ω = E[Jϕ ] + d3 x Jϕn (x)ϕn (x).                    (16.3.12)

Recalling Eq. (16.3.2) and the assumed form of J(x), this is
                                        Z                 
                           1               4    n             1
                  ⟨H⟩Ω =       −W [Jϕ ] + d x Jϕ (x)ϕn (x) = − Γ[ϕ].                (16.3.13)
                           T                                  T

As noted in the previous section, if the field ϕ(x) has a constant value ϕ over a large
spacetime volume V4 = V3 T , then we may write the effective action in terms of an effective
potential V (ϕ):
                                   Γ[ϕ] = −V3 T V (ϕ).                            (16.3.14)
In this case Eq. (16.3.13) tells us that the energy density is

                                          ⟨H⟩Ω /V3 = V (ϕ).                         (16.3.15)

     This is the main result: V (ϕ) is the minimum of the expectation value of the energy
density for all states constrained by the condition that the scalar fields Φn have expectation
values ϕn . One consequence is that in the absence of external currents the vacuum state
will relax to a state in which the potential V (ϕ) is not only stationary, which is required
by the field equations (16.1.8), but also a minimum.
     This result helps to resolve a problem in the interpretation of the quantum effective
potential. The Euclidean version of the path-integral formalism (described in Appendix
A of Chapter 23) makes it manifest that the two-point function ∆ is positive (in the ma-
trix sense), so according to Eq. (16.1.21) the same is true of −Π = ∆−1 . Together with
Eq. (16.2.3), this implies that for a single scalar field the effective potential V (ϕ) must
have a positive (or zero) second derivative with respect to ϕ. More generally, the effective
potential must be convex [5]:
                               
              V λϕ1 + (1 − λ)ϕ2 ≤ λV (ϕ1 ) + (1 − λ)V (ϕ2 ) for 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.

But inspection of Eq. (16.2.13) shows that for m2 < 0 and g > 0 the zero-loop approximation
to the effective potential for the scalar field theory with action (16.2.1) has a negative-
definite second derivative when ϕ is between the two minima of the effective potential
     p
at ± 6|m2 |/g. This contradiction arises because the derivation of perturbation theory




                                                  – 92 –
implicitly relies on the existence of a stable vacuum, but when V ′′ (ϕ) < 0, the field ϕ is at
a value of ϕ̄ where V (ϕ̄) − Jϕ ϕ̄ is a maximum rather than a minimum, which means that
the vacuum state in the presence of the current Jϕ is unstable.
     So what is the true effective potential for this scalar field theory when m2 < 0 and ϕ
lies between the two minima of the potential? The result of this section is that we must
find the state of minimum energy in which the expectation value of the operator Φ equals
ϕ. As long as ϕ is between the two minima of the potential, we can give Φ an expectation
value ϕ by taking the state as a suitable linear combination of the two states where ϕ is at
                    p
the minima ϕ ≃ ± 6|m2 |/g. The energy in this state is equal to the energy at the minima,
so this state clearly minimizes the energy. (Interference terms here vanish in the limit of
infinite volume, for reasons explained in Section 19.1.) Thus the effective potential between
the two minima of the potential is a constant, satisfying the requirement that it have a
nonpositive second derivative. The same argument shows that in more general theories
where the potential has two local minima of unequal energy, the potential between these
minima is linear [6].

16.4   Symmetries of the Effective Action
In some but not all cases, the symmetries of the action I[ϕ] are automatically also symme-
tries of the effective action Γ[ϕ]. For instance, in the example of Section 16.2, the action
(16.2.1) has a symmetry under the discrete transformation ϕ → −ϕ. Thus it follows from
their definition that Z[J] and W [J] are even under the corresponding reflection J → −J.
Eq. (16.1.5) then shows that ϕ−J = −ϕJ , and hence J−ϕ = −Jϕ , so Eq. (16.1.6) shows
that Γ[ϕ] is even under ϕ → −ϕ. This is borne out by the one-loop result (16.2.15). The
fermion-loop contribution in (16.2.16) also exhibits the symmetry under ϕ → −ϕ in the spe-
cial case where M (0) = 0, because in this case the action is invariant under the combined
transformation ϕ → −ϕ, ψ → γ5 ψ.
     We encounter problems in establishing the renormalizability of a theory, unless we can
show that the symmetries that we impose on the action also apply to the effective action.
For instance, in the example above, if I[ϕ] were assumed to be even in ϕ but Γ[ϕ] turned out
not to be, then the coefficients of the terms in Γ proportional to d4 x ϕ and d4 x ϕ3 would
                                                                  R          R

be divergent, but the symmetry of the action would not allow us to introduce counterterms
to absorb these infinities.
     With this motivation, let’s now turn to the important class of symmetries generated
by infinitesimal transformations

                                χn (x) −→ χn (x) + ϵF n [x; χ],                       (16.4.1)

where F n is a function of xµ that depends functionally on χn . (For instance, F n [x; χ] may
be an ordinary function of the χn and their derivatives at the point x.) We are now using
the symbol χn rather than ϕn to denote the different types of fields, to emphasize that
these include not only ordinary gauge and matter fields (which in the next chapter will
be denoted ϕr (x)), but all other fields appearing in the gauge-fixed action, including ghost
fields. We repeat that these χn (x) may be of any type, not necessarily scalars.

     Is this the symmetry transformation with which we started? It is for one very important

F is                                        Z

                           n          n

                                            Z

Hence Eq. (16.4.6) requires that Γ[χ] be invariant under all the functional linear transfor-

     We occasionally have to deal with symmetry transformations that are not linear. One
important example is provided by the BRST transformation discussed in Section 15.7. For
non-linear transformations, the symmetry transformation (16.4.7) under which the effec-
tive action is invariant is not generally the same as the assumed symmetry transformation
(16.4.1) that leaves the original action invariant, because the average of a non-linear func-
tional of fields is not generally the same as the functional of the average fields. Indeed, the
form of ⟨F ⟩Jχ as a functional of χ depends in general on the dynamics of the system, and is
usually non-local. This complication will be dealt with in the next chapter by the method
of antibrackets.

statistics. With currents inserted to the right of fields, as in Eqs. (16.1.1) and (16.4.5),

    Solutions to Weinberg Exercises
    These editorial solutions were added by Codex and are not part of Weinberg’s original text.

W.16.1. For a constant pseudoscalar background, the quadratic fermion operator contains a
        scalar mass m and a pseudoscalar mass gϕ. In the Hermitian pseudoscalar convention
        the latter is written igϕγ5 ; the factor i may instead be absorbed into the definition
        of the coupling used in the question. A constant chiral rotation combines the two
        masses into
                                           ρ2 (ϕ) = m2 + g 2 ϕ2 .
         Equivalently, multiplication of the Dirac operator by its conjugate converts its deter-
         minant to a determinant of −∂ 2 + ρ2 . There is no gauge field here, so this constant
         change of variables has no anomalous term.
         The scalar fluctuation determinant is independent of the background, since the scalar
         theory is otherwise free, and can be absorbed into the vacuum-energy counterterm.
         The fermion determinant has the form of the last term of Eq. (16.2.16), with M 2 (ϕ)
         replaced by ρ2 (ϕ). Thus, in the normalization used in this chapter,

                                          1         hR 4 ρ4 (ϕ) ρ2 (ϕ)
                           Veff (ϕ) = λR + MR2 ϕ2 +    ϕ −       ln
                                          2         24     32π 2    κ2

         through one loop, up to a scheme-dependent finite polynomial in ϕ2 . Here ρ2 (ϕ) =
         m2R + gR2 ϕ2 to the required accuracy. The scale κ merely makes the logarithm dimen-

         sionless.




                                              – 96 –
          Although no ϕ4 interaction was specified in the classical Lagrangian, the determinant
          contains divergences proportional to 1, ϕ2 , and ϕ4 . Renormalization therefore requires
          the vacuum, scalar-mass, and quartic counterterms displayed above; one may impose
          hR = 0 at a chosen subtraction scale, but it does not stay zero at every scale. If the
          coupling in the question is interpreted literally without the Hermiticity factor i, the
          same calculation gives the analytic continuation g 2 7→ −g 2 .

W.16.2. Use collective indices i = (n, x), j = (m, y), and so on, with repeated indices denoting
        both summation and spacetime integration. Write

                                        ∆ij = W,ij ,        Γij = Γ,ij .

          Differentiating the Legendre relations gives

                                              Γia ∆aj = −δij .

          Differentiation with respect to Jk , followed by multiplication by ∆, gives

                                         W,ijk = ∆ia ∆jb ∆kc Γabc .

          The sign is positive because the full connected two-point function in this chapter is
          already ∆ = −Γ(2)−1 .
          Differentiating once more, and using the three possible choices of the differentiated
          external propagator, yields
                                             
                     W,ijkl = ∆ia ∆jb ∆kc ∆ld Γabcd + Γabe ∆ef Γf cd
                                                                                          
                                                         + Γace ∆ef Γf bd + Γade ∆ef Γf bc .

          The first formula is the tree consisting of one full 1PI three-point vertex and three
          full external propagators. At four points the first term is one full 1PI four-point
          vertex. The other three terms are the s-, t-, and u-type trees made from two full 1PI
          three-point vertices joined by one full propagator; four full external propagators are
          attached in every term. These are precisely the connected trees generated by Γ.

W.16.3. In six dimensions the renormalizable classical potential must be allowed to contain

           Defining α Cα = iW [J] gives Z = eiW .
                    P

           A derivative of Z may act on different factors in its exponential, so it includes
           products of disconnected correlators. In contrast, derivatives of the exponent
           select insertions within the same connected component. Consequently W,i1 ···in
           generates connected n-point functions, with the conventional factors of i restored

       (b) Differentiate Γia ∆aj = −δij , where ∆ij = W,ij , with respect to Jk :

                                          W,ℓjk = ∆ℓi ∆ja ∆kb Γiab .

           Thus the connected three-point function is a single full 1PI cubic vertex with one
           full propagator attached to each external point. The displayed plus sign would
           look different if the minus sign were moved out of the definition ∆ = −Γ(2)−1 .

S.16.2. Convexity and Linear Symmetries of the Effective Action

        (a) In Euclidean signature, for every test function fi ,
                                    fi W,ij fj = (fi χi − ⟨fi χi ⟩)2 ≥ 0.
            After zero modes are regulated, ∆ = W (2) is positive and −Γ(2) = ∆−1 is
            positive in the convention of this chapter. For a constant scalar, Γ = −V4 V , so
            the zero-momentum kernel obeys
                                                V ′′ (ϕ) ≥ 0.
            With several scalars, the Hessian of V is positive semidefinite.
            A zero eigenvalue corresponds to a flat direction or to a limiting susceptibility
            and is handled by a regulated inverse or a Legendre–Fenchel transform. A loop
            expansion about an unstable homogeneous saddle does not perform the global
            minimization implicit in the exact transform, so any finite truncation may remain
            nonconvex.
        (b) The source pairing is preserved by
                                        ϕ 7→ M ϕ,      J 7→ M −T J,
            since (M ϕ)T M −T J = ϕT J. A change of integration variables therefore gives
                                           W [M −T J] = W [J].
            Differentiation and the chain rule yield
                                  ϕM −T J = M ϕJ ,       JM ϕ = M −T Jϕ .
            Consequently,
                                Γ[M ϕ] = −(M ϕ)T M −T Jϕ + W [M −T Jϕ ]
                                        = −ϕT Jϕ + W [Jϕ ] = Γ[ϕ].
            Orthogonality was never used; invertibility and invariance of action and measure
            suffice.
        (c) Changing variables ϕ 7→ −ϕ gives
                                   Z[J] = Z[−J],        W [J] = W [−J].
            Differentiation yields ϕ−J = −ϕJ , and inversion gives J−ϕ = −Jϕ . The Legendre
            transform then satisfies
                        Γ[−ϕ] = −(−ϕ)J−ϕ + W [J−ϕ ] = −ϕJϕ + W [Jϕ ] = Γ[ϕ].
            Taking an odd number of derivatives and setting ϕ = 0 therefore gives
                                              Γ(2r+1) (0) = 0.
            If one instead writes ϕ = v + η about a chosen nonzero minimum, the reflection
            exchanges the expansions about +v and −v; it is not simply η 7→ −η within one
            chosen phase. Odd vertices in η need not vanish.

           Such a homogeneous configuration is not a stable saddle about which an ordinary
           vacuum loop expansion is valid. The exact effective potential is defined by
           a constrained minimum energy and is real and convex. The imaginary part
           therefore diagnoses decay or spinodal instability of the perturbative branch; it
           is not an imaginary exact ground-state energy.

            with integration over x understood in the first term. A second derivative gives

            At the symmetric background ϕ = 0, the one-derivative identity says that Γ(2)
            commutes with every generator. The two-derivative identity similarly says that
            Γ(3) is an invariant rank-three tensor. More generally every 1PI vertex is an
            O(N )-invariant tensor.

      (c) Every vacuum graph in Z is a disjoint union of connected components. The

          subgraphs joined by exact propagators. The Legendre transform removes pre-
          cisely those tree connections: differentiating Γ produces the 1PI vertices, while
          reconnecting them with G = (Γ(2) )−1 reconstructs connected correlators.

                                    W (J; ϕ0 ) = W (J; 0) − Jϕ0 .

                         Γ(χ; ϕ0 ) = W (Jχ ; 0) − Jχ (ϕ0 + χ) = Γ(ϕ0 + χ; 0),

                                           – 119 –
17.2    Renormalization: Direct Analysis
The simplest non-Abelian gauge theories are renormalizable in the ‘Dyson’ sense that the
operators in the Lagrangian density all have dimensionality (in powers of mass) four or
less. As we saw in Chapter 12, this guarantees that the infinities in the quantum effective
action only appear in terms that could be cancelled by the counterterms in interactions
of dimensionality four or less. But there is more to renormalizability than this. The
Lagrangian density is constrained by gauge invariance and other symmetries. For a theory
to be renormalizable, it is necessary that the infinities in the quantum effective action satisfy
the same constraints, up to possible renormalizations of the fields.
     The effective action Γ[χ, K] is a complicated functional of both χ and K, about which
the symmetry condition (17.1.9) says complicated things, but fortunately matters are much
simpler for the infinite terms in Γ. We will write the action S[χ, K] = I[χ] + d4 x ∆n Kn as
                                                                                 R

the sum of a term SR [χ, K] in which masses and coupling constants are set equal to their
renormalized values, plus a correction S∞ [χ, K], which contains the counterterms that we
intend to cancel the infinities from loop graphs. Both SR and S∞ must be taken to have the
symmetries of the original action S[χ, K], so the question is whether the infinite parts of the
higher-order contributions to Γ share the same symmetries, so that they can be cancelled
by the counterterms in S∞ .
     We may expand Γ in a series of terms ΓN arising from diagrams with just N loops,
plus contributions from graphs with N − M loops (where 1 ≤ M ≤ N ) involving various
counterterms in S∞ [χ, K] that will be used to cancel infinities in graphs with a total of M
loops:
                                               X∞
                                    Γ[χ, K] =      ΓN [χ, K].                           (17.2.1)
                                                      N =0

This is a symmetry principle generated by SR , just like that described by Eqs. (15.9.16) and

fields Kn as well as the fields χn .
     Up to this point, we have used none of the special properties of a renormalizable Yang–
Mills theory. Now note that, according to the general power-counting rules of renormaliza-
tion theory, with all infinities cancelled in subgraphs of ΓN , the infinite part ΓN,∞ [χ, K]
of ΓN [χ, K] can only be a sum of products of fields (including K) and their derivatives
of dimensionality (in powers of mass) four or less. Finally, the arguments of Section 16.4
show that Γ[χ, K] and hence also ΓN,∞ [χ, K] are invariant under all of the linearly realized
symmetry transformations under which the action is invariant. (As described below, these
are: Lorentz transformations, global gauge transformations, antighost translations, and the
ghost phase transformations associated with ghost number conservation. Of course, the
auxiliary fields Kn must be assigned suitable transformation properties under these sym-
metry transformations.) These conditions together with Eq. (17.2.3) will suffice to tell us
all we need to know about the structure of ΓN,∞ [χ, K].
     To implement these conditions, we need to know the dimensionalities of the exter-
nal fields Kn . If a field χn has dimensionality dn (that is, dn powers of mass), then ∆n
correspondingly has dimensionality dn + 1 (as can be seen by inspection of the BRST trans-
formation rules (15.7.7)–(15.7.11)), so in order for d4 x Kn ∆n to be dimensionless, Kn
                                                       R

must have dimensionality 3 − dn . The fields Aαµ , ω α , and ω α∗ all have dimensionalities
dn = +1, so the corresponding Kn all have dimensionalities +2. (We do not introduce
any external field corresponding to hα , because this field is BRST-invariant.) Any spin
1/2 matter fields ψℓ have dimensionalities 3/2, and the corresponding Kn thus also have
dimensionalities 3/2. Thus a dimension four quantity like ΓN,∞ [χ, K] is at most quadratic
in any of the Kn . Furthermore terms that are of second order in the Kn cannot involve any
other fields, except that a term of second order in the Kn for spin 1/2 matter fields may
involve at most one additional field of dimensionality unity.
     We can now use ghost number conservation to show that in fact ΓN,∞ [χ, K] does not
contain any terms of second order in the Kn . For this purpose, we also need the ghost
quantum numbers of the Kn . If χn has ghost quantum number γn , then ∆n has ghost
quantum number γn + 1, so Kn must be assigned ghost quantum number −γn − 1. The
ghost quantum numbers of the fields Aαµ , ψ ℓ , ω α , and ω α∗ are respectively 0, 0, +1, and
−1, so the corresponding external fields Kn have ghost quantum numbers −1, −1, −2,
and 0, respectively. This rules out any terms in ΓN,∞ [χ, K] that are of second order in
the Kn , with the one possible exception of a term of second order in the external fields
Kα∗ associated with ω α∗ (and involving no other fields). However, these last terms are also
forbidden, for a different reason. The BRST transformation of ω α∗ is linear in the fields,

that is renormalizable, in the sense that it consists only of terms of dimensionality +4 or
less, that has these linearly acting symmetries, and that is invariant under the modified
BRST transformations (17.2.11)–(17.2.15).
     From Eq. (17.2.17) we may conclude that the fields Aµα , ωα , ωα∗ , and hα have the
dimensionalities +1, +1, +1, and +2, respectively (in powers of mass). Note also that
ghost number conservation requires that ω and ω ∗ come in pairs, while antighost translation
invariance dictates that ω ∗ always appears as a derivative. Each pair of ω and ∂µ ω ∗ fields
adds +3 to the dimensionality, so renormalizability rules out any term with more than one
such pair. With one such pair we can have at most one more derivative or one additional
gauge field, and Lorentz invariance dictates that we must have one or the other. The only
renormalizable allowed interactions involving ghost fields are then linear combinations of
terms of the form ∂µ ωα∗ ∂ µ ωβ or ∂µ ωα∗ Aµγ ωβ .
     Next, let us consider the terms that involve the field hα and possibly other fields but
not ω or ω ∗ . This field has dimensionality +2, so renormalizability and Lorentz invariance
allows this field to appear only29 multiplied with another hβ or ∂µ Aµβ or Aµβ Aγµ .
     Finally, the Lagrangian will contain renormalizable terms involving only the matter
and gauge fields. We will call the sum of these terms LψA . Putting this all together and
using global gauge invariance, the most general renormalizable interaction allowed by the
assumed symmetries (aside from BRST invariance) takes the form:

     In the above proof we made important use of the accidental invariance of the gauge-

important example is the background gauge-fixing functional to be introduced in Section

yield four-ghost interactions in the Lagrangian, so there are no counterterms available
to absorb ultraviolet divergences in this term. This is not just a technical obstacle to
proving renormalizability; for gauge-fixing functionals like fα = ∂µ Aµα + aαβγ Aµβ Aγµ , one-
loop graphs actually do yield divergences in four-ghost amplitudes that cannot be cancelled
by counterterms in the Faddeev–Popov–De Witt Lagrangian.
     Aside from avoiding gauge-fixing functionals other than fα = ∂µ Aµα , the only solution
to this problem seems to be the one mentioned in Section 15.7. We must give up the
Faddeev–Popov–De Witt approach, and instead take the action from the beginning as the
most general renormalizable function of the gauge, matter, ghost, and auxiliary fields that is
invariant under BRST and the other symmetries of the theory. According to the arguments
of Section 15.8, the action can be written in the form I0 + sΨ with I0 ghost-free, and the
S-matrix is independent of Ψ, so we can justify this procedure by quantizing the gauge
theory in axial gauge, where ghosts decouple, and then taking Ψ to be anything we like. In
particular, we can include s(ω ∗ ω ∗ ω) terms in the action that can serve as counterterms to
the divergences in four-ghost vertices.

17.3    Renormalization: General Gauge Theories30
The proof of the renormalizability of non-Abelian gauge theories in the previous section
relied on a ‘brute force’ analysis of the possible terms in the action of dimensionality four
or less. But as we saw in Chapter 12, this limitation on the dimensionality of terms in the
action can be at best a good approximation. The successful renormalizable quantum field
  30
    This section lies somewhat out of the book’s main line of development, and may be omitted in a first
reading.




                                               – 127 –
theories that are used to describe the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions are
almost certainly effective field theories, accompanied with terms of dimensionality d > 4;
these terms are normally not observed because they are suppressed by 4 − d powers of
some very large mass, perhaps of order 1016 –1018 GeV. Gravitation too can be described by
an effective field theory, in which the Lagrangian density contains not only the Einstein–
                 √
Hilbert term − gR/16πG, but also all scalars constructed from four or more derivatives
of the gravitational field. We need to show that gauge theories of this sort, which are not
renormalizable in the power-counting sense, are nonetheless renormalizable in the modern
sense that the ultraviolet divergences are governed by the gauge symmetries in such a way
that there is a counterterm available to cancel every infinity [3].
     For this purpose, let us return to the action S[χ, χ‡ ] introduced in Section 15.9, taken
as a function of independent fields χn (including gauge and matter fields ϕr and ghost
fields ω A as well as the non-minimal fields ω ∗A and hA ), together with their antifields χ‡n .
In theories like quantum gravity or Yang–Mills theories, that are based on a closed gauge
algebra with structure constants f C AB , this action is constrained to be of the form

G(t) −→ G(t + δt) = G(t) + (F (t)δt, G(t)) (where G(t) is any functional of fields and
antifields, and F (t) is the generating functional) leads to a finite canonical transformation
G −→ G  e ≡ G(1), with

                              dt

                                   F (t) = gtF1 + ℏ2 t2 F2 + · · · ,                   (17.3.7)

then Eqs. (17.3.3), (17.3.6), and (17.3.7) yield a transformed action

The question is whether we can use what freedom we have to choose the FN and SN so as
to cancel all infinities arising from loop graphs.
     As already noted, the first term SR in Eq. (17.3.3) is automatically finite. Suppose
that by cancellation of infinities with SM and FM for M < N it has been possible to
eliminate all infinities in the terms ΓM of order ℏM in the quantum effective action with
M < N . As we saw in the previous section, the Zinn–Justin equation (derived here by
setting χ‡n = Kn + δΨ/δχn ) tells us in this case that the infinite part ΓN,∞ of the term in
the quantum effective action of order ℏN satisfies the condition

                                          (SR , ΓN,∞ ) = 0.                            (17.3.9)

The field and antifield variables χn and χ‡n are related to the variables χn and Kn by
an anticanonical transformation, which preserves all antibrackets, so the antibracket in
Eq. (17.3.9) may be calculated in terms of χn and χ‡n instead of χn and Kn .
     The condition (17.3.5) satisfied by the counterterm SN is not the same as the condition
(17.3.9) satisfied by ΓN,∞ . However, given any SN 0 that satisfies Eq. (17.3.5), we can find a

class of other solutions

          X2 = S20 + 2(F1 , S1 ) + (F1 , (F1 , SR )) + two-loop terms involving only SR

For our purposes the only thing we need to know about XN is that it does not involve SN  ′

or FN , and that it is invariant under any linearly realized global symmetries of SR .
    Now, because (SR , SR ) = 0, the operation F 7−→ (SR , F ) is nilpotent; for all F ,

                                           (SR , (SR , F )) = 0.                                 (17.3.13)

Hence it follows from Eqs. (17.3.9) and (17.3.11)–(17.3.13) that

                                            (SR , XN,∞ ) = 0.                                    (17.3.14)

Any term in XN,∞ of the form (SR , Y ) may be cancelled in Eq. (17.3.12) by choosing FN,∞
equal to Y . Thus the space of possible remaining infinite terms in XN,∞ that need to be
cancelled by the counterterm SN,∞′   consist of those functionals X that satisfy (SR , X) = 0,
counting as equivalent functionals that differ only by terms of the form (SR , Y ). In other
words, the infinities in ΓN that need to be cancelled by the counterterms SN  ′ belong to the

cohomology of the mapping X 7−→ (SR , X).
     The possible form of the counterterm SN  ′ is limited by the requirement that S + S ′
                                                                                       R     N
must satisfy whatever structural constraints are imposed on the action S. Thus we can
complete the proof of renormalizability if we can show that the cohomology of the mapping
X 7−→ (SR , X) consists only of functionals that satisfy this structural constraint.
     In the case of quantum gravity coupled to the Yang–Mills fields of a semisimple gauge
symmetry, the symmetries of the theory are implemented by the structural constraint
(17.3.1). In this case there is a theorem [4] that states that the cohomology of the map-
ping X 7−→ (SR , X) (on the space of local functionals, rather than spacetime-dependent
functions, of ghost number zero) consists 31 of functionals A[ϕ] that are invariant under the
gauge transformation ϕr −→ ϕr + ϵA fAr [ϕ] with structure constants f C AB . Any N th-order
infinity of this sort may be cancelled with a counterterm SN ′ of the same form, so although

these theories are not renormalizable in the conventional power-counting sense, they are
renormalizable in the sense that all infinities can be eliminated by a choice of parameters
in the original bare action I[ϕ] and by a suitable renormalization of fields and antifields.
     In other theories the cohomology of the map X 7−→ (SR , X) contains additional terms.
This does not necessarily require a weakening of the structural constraints, because the
  31
    Strictly speaking, this is valid if one requires that the constant coefficients in S do not take special
values for which S would be invariant under a larger group of local symmetries. For instance, this excludes
the case S = 0.




                                                 – 130 –
additional terms in the cohomology may not correspond to actual ultraviolet divergences.
For instance, in gauge theories with U (1) factors the cohomology contains terms [4] corre-
sponding to a redefinition of the action of the U (1) gauge symmetry on the various fields
of the theory, which if infinite would require us to weaken the structural constraints by
leaving the normalization of the transformation functions fAr [ϕ] in Eq. (17.3.1) arbitrary.
But this infinity is forbidden by the same soft-photon theorems that tell us that ratios of
U (1) couplings to various fields (like the ratios of the various lepton charges in quantum
electrodynamics) are unaffected by radiative corrections. (See Section 10.4.) Where the
extra terms in the cohomology do contain ultraviolet divergences, it is necessary to weaken
the structural constraint imposed on S in order that there should be a counterterm for
every possible ultraviolet divergence. It is not known whether this will always be possi-
ble; if not, some theories may have to be rejected because of their unremovable ultraviolet
divergences.

17.4    Background Field Gauge
We next turn to a method of calculation that explicitly preserves a sort of gauge invariance,
and that therefore proves extremely convenient, especially in one-loop calculations. We
consider the effective action Γ[A, ψ, ω, ω ∗ ] as a functional32 of classical external gauge,
matter, ghost and antighost fields: Aαµ (x), ψℓ (x), ωα (x), ωα∗ (x). Even though ghosts and
antighosts never appear in initial or final states, we are considering background ghost and
antighost fields as well as gauge and matter fields in order to deal with parts of diagrams
that have external ghost or antighost lines.
     As described in Section 16.1, Γ[A, ψ, ω, ω ∗ ] is the sum of connected one-particle-
irreducible graphs for the vacuum–vacuum amplitude, calculated in a theory in which
the quantum fields A′ , ψ ′ , ω ′ , ω ′∗ over which we integrate are replaced in the action
with shifted fields A + A′ , ψ + ψ ′ , ω + ω ′ , ω ∗ + ω ′∗ , the path integral being taken over
primed fields with the unprimed fields held fixed. We are free to choose the gauge-fixing
function fα (x) pretty much any way we like; instead of our previous choice fα = ∂µ Aµα (or

involve the field strength in its original form (17.4.31), and so we can calculate the charge
renormalization factor by studying just one gauge field amplitude.

17.5    A One–Loop Calculation in Background Field Gauge
As an exercise, we are now going to calculate the one-loop renormalization factor for the
gauge coupling constant in a general non-Abelian gauge theory. As we will see in the
next chapter, this provides an essential input in so-called ‘renormalization group’ calcula-
tions of physical processes at high energy; the results we obtain here will be used there to
demonstrate the asymptotic freedom of non-Abelian gauge theories.
     The method to be employed here is somewhat novel. Usually, one considers the ef-
fective action in a spacetime-dependent background gauge field, and calculates the terms
quadratic in this field, extracting a factor (qµ Aαν − qν Aαµ )2 (where q is the gauge field
four-momentum), and only then isolating the logarithmic divergence by setting q = 0 in
the coefficient of this factor. Instead we shall follow the much simpler course of taking the
gauge field to be spacetime-independent from the beginning. In this case the terms in the
effective action that are quadratic or cubic in the gauge field of course vanish, but there is a
non-vanishing quartic term that is ultraviolet divergent, and which can be used to calculate
the coupling constant renormalization factor (1 + LA )−1/2 . In this way our one-loop calcu-
lation becomes a matter of simple matrix algebra. Note that this procedure can only work
in background field gauge; otherwise there would be independent logarithmic divergences
in the parts of the effective action that are quartic and quadratic in the background gauge
field.
     With this motivation, we turn to the calculation of the one-loop effective action in a
background field for which Aαµ is constant and ψ = ω = ω ∗ = 0. For such a background
field, the full modified Lagrangian is34

     Let us now (for the first time in this section) use the assumed simplicity of the gauge

                                          Cγαβ = gϵγαβ

with α, β, and γ running over the values 1, 2, 3. Comparing with Eq. (17.5.33), we see that
here
                                          C1 = 2.
Also in this theory the matter field forms a doublet with tα given by g/2 times the usual
Pauli matrix σα , so
                                         C2 = 1/2.
Somewhat more generally, for the group SU (N ) with nf fermions in the defining represen-
tation, with a conventional normalization of generators, we have35

    Weinberg Exercises
W.17.1. Carry out the proof of renormalizability given in Section 17.2, including elementary
        scalar fields in the Lagrangian.

W.17.2. Carry out the quantization of a non-Abelian gauge theory in background field gauge,
        using the BRST method of quantization discussed at the end of Section 17.2.

W.17.3. Derive the relation (17.5.44) between the renormalized and unrenormalized gauge
        couplings by calculating the terms in Γ(1 loop) that are quadratic in a spacetime-
        dependent gauge field.

W.17.4. Calculate the one-loop relation between the renormalized and unrenormalized gauge
        couplings in a gauge theory containing elementary scalar fields.

    Solutions to Weinberg Exercises
    These editorial solutions were added by Codex and are not part of Weinberg’s original text.

W.17.1. Let ϕi be real elementary scalars in a (possibly reducible) representation of the gauge
        algebra. It is useful to choose antisymmetric Hermitian generators Tα , including the
        coupling in the same way as the chapter’s tα , and to add to the BRST transformations

                               sϕi = iω α (Tα )i j ϕj ,     [Tα , Tβ ] = iCγαβ Tγ .

          The Jacobi identity and the representation relation give s2 ϕi = 0. Introduce a source
          Kϕi for sϕi . Since [ϕ] = 1, it has

                                        [Kϕ ] = 2,        gh(Kϕ ) = −1,

          and statistics opposite to those of ϕ.
          The loopwise Zinn–Justin argument is unchanged. Once subdivergences through N −
          1 loops have been subtracted, locality and power counting imply that ΓN,∞ is an
          integrated polynomial of dimension at most four. Its antifield-dependent part is at
          most linear in Kϕ : a term quadratic in Kϕ already has dimension four and ghost
          number −2, while no field of positive ghost number can be added without exceeding
          dimension four. Mixed quadratic terms are excluded by the same dimension and
          ghost-number counting used in Section 17.2. Thus
                                              Z
                        ΓN,∞ = ΓN,∞ [χ, 0] + d4 x Kn DN n
                                                          ,    (SR , ΓN,∞ ) = 0.




                                                  – 144 –
         The last equation says that the action and the BRST transformation are infinitesi-
         mally deformed together, and that the deformed transformation is nilpotent.
         Lorentz covariance, ghost number, and dimension now restrict the scalar part of that
         deformation to
                                       s′ ϕi = iZω α (Tα′ )i j ϕj ,
         apart from a possible transformation of a constant scalar shift when the fields are
         expanded about a vacuum. Nilpotence requires
                                                [Tα′ , Tβ′ ] = iCγαβ
                                                                 ′
                                                                     Tγ′ .
         Hence Tα′ is the same representation after a change of scalar basis and the common
         gauge-coupling renormalization already found for the gauge and fermion sectors. For
         repeated equivalent irreducible representations, the allowed change of basis is a matrix
         wave-function renormalization among the copies.
         It remains to classify the scalar-dependent part of the local action. Before gauge
         fixing, the most general renormalizable expression is
                                      1                            1
                             Lϕ = − Zij (Dµ ϕ)i (Dµ ϕ)j − ai ϕi − m2ij ϕi ϕj
                                      2                            2
                                       1             1
                                   − κijk ϕi ϕj ϕk − λijkl ϕi ϕj ϕk ϕl ,
                                      3!            4!
         supplemented, when fermions are present, by every gauge-invariant Yukawa tensor
         Y i . Gauge invariance says, for example,
                             ′                  ′                   ′                 ′
                      (Tα )i i λi′ jkl + (Tα )j j λij ′ kl + (Tα )k k λijk′ l + (Tα )l l λijkl′ = 0,
         with analogous equations for a, m2 , κ, and Y . These are precisely the tensors available
         as counterterms.
         Finally, scalar fields enlarge the renormalizable gauge-fixing fermion. Depending on
         the gauge, it may contain ωα∗ uαi ϕi or ωα∗ uαij ϕi ϕj ; after applying s these generate
         the hϕ and hϕϕ terms mentioned in Section 17.2, together with their required ghost
         partners. They are BRST-exact and are absorbed by renormalizing the gauge-fixing
         fermion. Therefore all possible divergences are removed by scalar wave-function,
         potential, Yukawa, gauge-coupling, and BRST-exact gauge-fixing counterterms. The
         induction closes, provided the matter representation is anomaly free and the regulator
         preserves, or is corrected to restore, the Zinn–Justin identity.

W.17.2. Write the full gauge field as Aαµ = Aαµ + A′αµ , where A is the prescribed background
        and A′ is integrated over. The quantum BRST differential leaves the background
        fixed and is obtained from the true gauge transformation (17.4.17) by replacing its
        parameter by the ghost:
                                 sAαµ = 0,
                                 sA′αµ = D̄µ ωα − Cαβγ ωβ A′γµ ,
                                           1
                                  sωα = − Cαβγ ωβ ωγ ,
                                           2
                                     ∗
                                  sωα = −hα ,                    shα = 0.




                                                    – 145 –
         Here D̄µ contains only A. On a quantum matter fluctuation, sψ ′ = itα ωα (ψ + ψ ′ ),
         while sψ = 0. These rules are nilpotent because their action on the sums A + A′ and
         ψ + ψ ′ is the ordinary Yang–Mills BRST differential.
         Choose the background-covariant gauge-fixing fermion
                                      Z                      
                                          4   ∗     µ ′     ξ
                               Ψ = − d x ωα D̄ Aαµ + hα .
                                                            2
         Up to the harmless overall sign convention for s, its variation is
                                 Z      n                 ξ
                           sΨ = d4 x hα D̄µ A′αµ + hα hα
                                                          2
                                                                             o
                                          + ωα∗ D̄µ [ D̄µ ωα − Cαβγ ωβ A′γµ ] .

         Eliminating hα gives −(D̄µ A′αµ )2 /(2ξ), while the last line is precisely the background-
         gauge Faddeev–Popov operator. Thus the gauge-fixed action is

                                      Sgf = I0 [A + A′ , ψ + ψ ′ ] + sΨ.

         Adding sources Kn for the nonlinear quantum BRST variations gives the usual Zinn–
         Justin identity (Γ, Γ) = 0, so the direct renormalization argument applies even though
         antighost translation is no longer available; one simply admits the full set of local
         BRST-exact counterterms sΨct .
         There is in addition a background gauge transformation. The background A trans-
         forms as a connection, while A′ , ω, ω ∗ , and h transform homogeneously in the adjoint
         representation (and both background and quantum matter transform in their matter
         representation). Consequently D̄µ A′µ transforms homogeneously, Ψ and sΨ are in-
         variant, and the functional measure may be chosen invariant. The effective action of
         the background fields therefore obeys an ordinary background Ward identity.
         In particular, its divergent pure-background term has the form
                                                 Z
                                            1
                                 Γ∞ [A] ⊃ − LA d4 x Fαµν [A]Fα µν [A].
                                            4

         Defining AR = (1 + LA )1/2 A, background gauge invariance requires the product of
         the coupling and the background connection to remain fixed:
                                                                   1/2
                                  g R = g(1 + LA )−1/2 ,      Zg ZA = 1.

         This is the practical advantage of the construction: the coupling counterterm is ob-
         tained from the background two-point function alone.

                                 Z

                                 P
       (a) Substitution of Γ =       N ΓN into (Γ, Γ) = 0 gives at total loop order N

                                              N

                                              r=0

           Suppose all lower-order divergences and subdivergences have been canceled. In
           the pole part of this equation, every term with 0 < r < N is finite. Only the
           two equal endpoint terms can contain the remaining overall divergence:

                                        (SR , ΓN,∞ ) + (ΓN,∞ , SR ) = 0.

           Since both entries are even, the two terms are equal in the chapter’s antibracket
           convention. Therefore
                                            (SR , ΓN,∞ ) = 0.
           Locality of ΓN,∞ follows from the subtraction of all subdivergences.
       (b) An odd functional F generates the infinitesimal anticanonical transformation

                                     δχn = (χn , F ),        δKn = (Kn , F ).

           The induced change of S is

                                          δS = (S, F ) = BS F = Σ.

           Anticanonical transformations preserve the antibracket, so the master equation
           remains true. If F is linear in the antifields it is an ordinary local field re-
           definition, with the compensating inverse transformation of sources. If F is a
           change of gauge-fixing fermion, its effect is s δΨ. In either case the cocycle is
           exact: it changes coordinates or gauge choice, not the coefficient of a nontrivial
           gauge-invariant operator.

S.17.3. Scalar BRST Cohomology and Power Counting


       (a) The undifferentiated A2 term makes the ghost action depend on ω ∗ without a
           derivative, so a constant antighost shift is no longer a symmetry. Since

                                      [ω ∗ A2 ] = 3,     gh(ω ∗ A2 ) = −1,

           its BRST variation is an allowed dimension-four, ghost-number-zero interaction.
           Likewise
                                   [ω ∗ ω ∗ ω] = 3,       gh(ω ∗ ω ∗ ω) = −1,

           so

                                   s(ωα∗ ωβ∗ ωγ ) = − hα ωβ∗ ωγ + ωα∗ hβ ωγ
                                                      1
                                                    − Cγδϵ ωα∗ ωβ∗ ωδ ωϵ
                                                      2
           is also allowed. The last term is a four-ghost vertex absent from the minimal
           Faddeev–Popov action, yet no remaining symmetry forbids its divergent coeffi-
           cient. Closure under renormalization therefore requires starting from the general
           BRST-invariant action I0 + sΨ, with this interaction available as a counterterm.
       (b) Using the odd Leibniz rule,

                                 s2 ϕ = i(sω α )Tα ϕ − iω α Tα (sϕ)
                                          i
                                      = − Cαβγ ω β ω γ Tα ϕ + ω α ω β Tα Tβ ϕ
                                          2
                                        1 α β
                                      = ω ω ([Tα , Tβ ] − iCγαβ Tγ ) ϕ.
                                        2

           Thus s2 ϕ = 0 for arbitrary ghosts precisely when [Tα , Tβ ] = iCγαβ Tγ . Con-
           versely, if nilpotence holds on a faithful collection of scalar fields, the coefficient
           of each independent ω α ω β vanishes and gives the representation relation.
       (c) The scalar source has dimension two, ghost number −1, and odd parity. Two
           such sources already have dimension four, so the only candidate is Kϕi Kϕj , with
           an antisymmetric coefficient if the sources are distinct. Its ghost number is −2, so
           it is forbidden. The mixed dimension-four candidates with other dimension-two
           sources are
                                     Kϕ KA ,          K ϕ Kω ,    Kϕ Kω∗ .

           Their ghost numbers are respectively −2, −3, −1. Adding a ghost to repair the
           last value would raise the dimension to five. The product Kϕ Kψ has dimension
           7/2, ghost number −2, and an uncontracted spinor index; a field that contracts
           it makes the dimension exceed four. Hence no local Lorentz scalar of dimension
           at most four and ghost number zero is quadratic in Kϕ or mixes Kϕ with another
           BRST source.

S.17.4. Slavnov Stability under Renormalization

       Write the broken identity at the first nonvanishing order as
                                     1
                                       (Γ, Γ) = ℏN AN + O(ℏN +1 ).
                                     2
       Applying the antibracket with Γ and using the Jacobi identity gives (Γ, (Γ, Γ)) = 0.
       At order N , lower orders may be replaced by SR , so

                                          BSR AN = (SR , AN ) = 0.

       If AN = BSR XN for a local ghost-number-zero functional XN , adding the counterterm
       −ℏN XN restores the identity. A closed but non-exact ghost-number-one local func-
       tional is a gauge anomaly. Its cohomology class, rather than a regulator-dependent
       representative, is the obstruction.

        (a) Write
