must be integrated over, with some weight function that depends on the process under

large µ by Eq. (18.7.7) as

     Despite initial hopes, the discovery of instantons has not led to much improvement in
our ability to do quantitative calculations in quantum chromodynamics. On the other hand,
as we shall now see, it has produced spectacular qualitative changes in our understanding
of quantum chromodynamics and other gauge theories.
     The mere fact that there are solutions of the field equations for which the integral
(23.5.15) does not vanish is enough to provide a solution of the U (1) problem discussed
in Section 19.10. Under global U (1) transformations ψ → exp(iγ5 α)ψ, the measure for
integration over quark fields undergoes a change given by Eq. (22.2.10):

gauge field that vanishes sufficiently rapidly at infinity. The instanton solution vanishes
only as 1/r, and yields a non-vanishing value for this integral, given by Eqs. (23.5.22),

showing that the anomaly does violate the U (1) chiral symmetry.
    As we saw in Section 22.4, the currents of baryon and lepton number also contain
anomalies due to the interaction of quarks and leptons with the SU (2) × U (1) gauge fields
of the standard model. Instanton configurations of the SU (2) gauge field therefore pro-
duce violations of baryon and lepton conservation. [25] As noted in Section 22.4, there are
various currents whose conservation is not violated by anomalies or anything else, such as
baryon number minus lepton number, and the differences of electron, muon, and tau lepton
numbers, so these will be conserved in any baryon- and lepton-non-conserving process. For




                                           – 546 –
instance, the decay of a proton or deuteron is forbidden, but the decay He3 → e+ +µ+ +ν τ is
allowed. The amplitudes for these effects are suppressed by the same factor exp(−8|ν|π 2 /g 2 )
as before, but now with g the SU (2) coupling constant e/ sin θ, evaluated not at a sliding
scale but at the natural scale for electroweak processes, roughly of order mZ . Taking
e2 /4π = 1/129 (see Section 18.2) and sin2 θ = 0.23, the suppression factor for |ν| = 1 is
exp(−373). He3 decay into three antileptons is not likely to be observed.

    There is another approach [26] that illuminates some aspects of instantons. In temporal
gauge, with Aα4 (x, x4 ) = 0, the gauge field for x4 → ±∞ is expected to approach time-
independent pure gauges for x4 → ±∞:

                                                            −1
                           iA(x, x4 ) ≡ itα Aα (x, x4 ) −→ g±  (x)∇g± (x),              (23.5.24)

where g± (x) are group elements in the representation generated by tα . Assuming that
Aα (x, x4 ) vanishes for x → ∞, the group elements g± (x) must approach constants g±
for x → ∞, so the three-spaces at x4 → ∞ may be regarded as three-spheres, with the
point at infinity regarded as an ordinary point. Following the same argument that led to
Eq. (23.4.13), we then have
            Z

where n± are integers. The integral over the boundary of four-space in Eq. (23.5.2) may
be regarded as the integral over the ‘plane’ x4 = +∞ minus the integral over the ‘plane’
x4 = −∞, so from (23.5.8) and (23.5.18) (with N = 1) we have

                                            ν = n+ − n− .                               (23.5.26)

The exponential factor exp(−8|ν|π 2 /g 2 ) from Eq. (23.5.19) may therefore be regarded as
the amplitude for a transition from a configuration with spatial winding number n− at
x4 → −∞ to one of spatial winding number n+ at x4 → +∞. The exponential form of this
factor for ν ̸= 0 reflects the fact that this is a tunneling process; no continuous sequence
of pure gauge fields can take us from a configuration of one spatial winding number to a
configuration with a different spatial winding number.
    The interpretation of the factor exp(−8|ν|π 2 /g 2 ) as a tunneling amplitude suggests that
baryon- and lepton-non-conserving processes may proceed rapidly at temperatures above
about 1 TeV, where instead of having to tunnel through the barrier, thermal fluctuations
can take the vacuum over the barrier. [27] This process may be of cosmological importance,
but it is still subject to the selection rules mentioned above: thermal fluctuations will
not change the density of baryon number minus lepton number, or the differences of the
densities of the three varieties of lepton number.

     The inclusion of a term (23.6.6) in the Lagrangian density would violate P and CP

violated by the weak interactions.

     This discussion shows that if any of the quark masses were to vanish, then the theta
angle would have no effect and there would be no P or CP non-conservation in quantum
chromodynamics. The analysis of quark mass ratios in Section 19.7 indicates that the
quarks all have non-zero masses, though it is sometimes suggested that the inclusion of
terms of second order in ms in this analysis might allow mu to vanish. [28] But there is no
question that the u and d quarks are quite light, which leads to some suppression of the
effects of a non-zero theta angle. We saw in Section 19.4 that mu and md are roughly of
order m2π /mN (where mN is used here as a typical quantum chromodynamic mass scale),
so we might expect the effects of the theta angle to be suppressed by four factors of mπ ,
but this is not quite correct. With P and CP not conserved there would be a non-zero
amplitude for the π 0 to disappear into the vacuum, proportional to m4π , but the ‘tadpole’
graphs with pion lines ending in such vacuum transition vertices would be enhanced by a
factor m−2                                                                    2        4
          π from the pion propagator, giving a net effect proportional to mπ , not mπ . In
particular, if we define fermion fields so that all Mf are real, then a non-zero theta angle
would produce a P - and T -non-conserving neutron electric dipole moment proportional to
|θ| and m2π , and hence on dimensional grounds of order [29]

                             dn ≈ |θ|em2π /m3N ≈ 10−16 |θ| e cm.                   (23.6.13)

The neutron electric dipole moment is known to be less than about 10−25 e cm, so |θ| < 10−9 .
     In order to explain in a natural way why θ is so small, Peccei and Quinn [30] proposed
a theory in which θ became in effect a dynamical variable, which could relax to a minimum
of the effective potential, at which P and CP would be conserved. Their idea was taken up
by Wilczek and myself, [31] who noted that it would require the existence of a light spinless
particle, the axion. The axion that appeared in the original Peccei–Quinn model has been
ruled out by experiment, but there are more general possibilities, [32] in which the axion
couples too weakly to ordinary matter to have been observed.
     The common feature of all versions of the axion theory is that there is some U (1)
symmetry that is spontaneously broken at energies much higher than those associated with
quantum chromodynamics, and is also broken by an anomaly involving the gluon fields.
According to the general formalism of Chapters 19 and 22, the low energy effective field
theory will contain a Goldstone boson field ϕ, so that, under the symmetry transformation

                                      ϕ −→ ϕ + Fϕ ϵ,                               (23.6.14)

the effective Lagrangian undergoes the transformation

defined to make the mass parameters Mf all real; otherwise observables will depend on
      P

of both P and CP . In the real world P and CP are not exact, but the only observed
violations are in the weak interactions, and would shift the expectation value of ϕ only a
small way [33] from −M θ.

     We can also use this formalism to say something about the interactions of axions with
hadrons. The eigenvector of M20 with eigenvalue m2a has a component along the original
π 0 direction equal to (mu cu − md cd )Fπ /(mu + md )M . As mentioned earlier, because of the
one-pion pole this is the dominant axion-hadron coupling. We see that the ratio of the axion
and pion production interaction amplitudes will typically be of order Fπ /M . The fact that
axions are not observed in such collisions indicates that M > 3 TeV, in contradiction with
the original expectation [30], [31] that the anomalous U (1) symmetry is spontaneously
broken by the same scalar vacuum expectation values of order 0.3 TeV that break the




                                                – 552 –
electroweak SU (2) × U (1) symmetry. It is possible to explain why axions are not found in
reactor or accelerator experiments by taking M as an independent parameter, [32] much
larger than the electroweak breaking scale, but there are still astrophysical limitations.
Limits on the rate of cooling of red giant stars give [34] M > 107 GeV, while observations
of the supernova SN1987A indicate [35] that M > 1010 GeV.120 Cosmological arguments
suggest [36] an upper bound M < 1012 GeV, leaving an open but narrow window of allowed
axion parameters.

23.7    Quantum Fluctuations around Extended Field Configurations

Topologically non-trivial four-dimensional field configurations such as instantons provide
only zeroth-order contributions to path integrals. Now we must consider the effect of
quantum fluctuations around these configurations.
     To start in a very general way, consider a set of fields, collectively called ϕ(x), whose dy-
namics is described by the Euclidean action I[ϕ], and suppose we have a set of configurations
ϕν,u at which I[ϕ] is stationary, where ν labels the topological type of the configuration, and
u represents a set of continuous collective parameters on which the configuration depends.
For instance, for instantons ν is the winding number, an integer, and u includes the position
and scale as well as its ‘direction’ in the gauge group. Euclidean path integrals may then
be written        Z                     XZ        Z
                                               du [dϕ′ ] exp I[ϕν,u + ϕ′ ] O,

only over fluctuations that do not entail changes in the collective parameters, and O stands
for any product of local functions of field operators. Because I[ϕ] is stationary at ϕ = ϕν,u ,
its expansion to second order in the fluctuations takes the form

the prime here indicating that we are to exclude the ‘zero modes’, the zero eigenvalues of

      These remarks allow us to refine the results given in Section 23.5 for the coupling-
constant dependence of instanton contributions with different winding numbers. Suppose
we define the fields of our theory in such a way that the action takes the form I[ϕ, g] =
g −2 I1 [ϕ], where I1 [ϕ] is independent of coupling constants. (For instance, as discussed at
the end of Section 15.2, in Yang–Mills theories we would use as a gauge field the canonically
normalized gauge field times a factor g.) Then all eigenvalues of K are proportional to g −2 ,
and the factor (23.7.3) is proportional to g to a power equal to the number of non-zero
eigenvalues of K. This power is of course infinite, but it can be written as the number of all
eigenvalues of K, which is also infinite but is independent of ν, minus the number N (ν) of
zero modes, equal to the number of collective parameters, which is finite and dependent on
ν. We conclude then that aside from factors that do not depend on ν, the contribution of
fluctuations around configurations of topological type ν is a factor with a coupling-constant
dependence that is given in terms of the number N (ν) of collective parameters by

                                           g −N (ν) .                                 (23.7.4)

This estimate is based on the approximation (23.7.2), which corresponds to a one-loop
approximation, so when higher-order terms are taken into account the factor (23.7.4) will
be multiplied with a power series in g, whose details depend on the operators O appearing
in the path integral.
     Let’s see how this applies to instantons. The configuration with ν = 0 of course has
no collective parameters, and so its contribution to path integrals is just a power series
in g. The configuration with ν = 1 has four collective parameters giving the spacetime
location of the instanton, one collective parameter giving the scale of the instanton, and
a number N1 of collective parameters corresponding to the rotations and/or global gauge
group transformations that do not leave the instanton invariant, so (now including the factor
exp(Iν ) given by Eq. (23.5.19)), the coupling-constant dependence for ν = 1 instantons is
g −5−N1 exp(−8π 2 /g 2 ). For the ν = 1 instanton (23.5.12) in an SU (2) Yang–Mills theory,
there are three independent rotations and three independent SU (2) transformations, but
since the instanton is invariant under three combined rotations and SU (2) transformations,
we have N1 = 3, so fluctuations around the ν = 1 instanton yield a coupling-constant
dependence g −8 exp(−8π 2 /g 2 ). In an SU (3) Yang–Mills theory we have three independent
rotations and eight independent SU (3) transformations, but again the instanton is invariant
under three independent combined rotations and SU (3) transformations in the standard
SU (2) subgroup (say, acting on the first two components of the defining representation
of SU (3)), and now also invariant under one additional SU (3) transformation that (like
hypercharge) commutes with all generators of the standard SU (2) subgroup. Hence N1 =
3+8−3−1 = 7, and the ν = 1 instanton yields a factor proportional to g −12 exp(−8π 2 /g 2 ).

    Now suppose that the action I also contains a term
                          Z      Z

                              4



involving independent fermion fields ψ and ψ̄. If none of these fields appear in O then
the integral over these fields yields a factor Det K(ν, u), which vanishes if K(ν, u) has any
zero modes. This result can be simply understood in terms of the rules for integration over
fermionic parameters. By expanding ψ(x) and ψ̄(x) in the eigenmodes of K, we can write
the integral over ψ(x) and ψ̄(x) as an integral over the coefficients in these expansions. The
coefficients of the zero modes do not appear in the quadratic approximation to the action, so
for each such fermionic zero mode we have an integral over a fermionic parameter that does
not appear in the integrand, which vanishes according to the general rules of Section 9.5.
The only terms in an integral over fermionic variables that do not vanish are those for which
the integrand contains a single factor of each integrated variable. Hence the integral over
fermionic fields in Eq. (23.7.1) will not vanish only if there is a single fermionic field in O
for each zero mode of K. For instantons there are fermionic zero modes whose numbers and
chiralities are governed by index theorems, like the Atiyah–Singer index theorem derived
in Section 22.2, so only certain processes are allowed for a given winding number. It was
on this basis that ’t Hooft [25] showed that the baryon- and lepton-nonconserving effective
interaction produced by ν = 1 instantons in the electroweak standard model must involve
just one of each lepton flavor.

23.8   Vacuum Decay
A vacuum state is stable if its scalar field expectation values are at a true minimum of
the effective potential. But if the scalar field expectation values are at a local minimum
that is higher than the true minimum then this vacuum will be metastable. A metastable
‘false’ vacuum state corresponding to a local minimum will decay into the stable ‘true’
vacuum corresponding to the true minimum by a process of barrier penetration, analogous
to nuclear alpha decay or spontaneous fission. This is not a process that can be observed in
our laboratories, but it has presumably occurred several times in the history of the universe
as various symmetries have become spontaneously broken, so it is important to be able to
calculate the rate of such false vacuum decay. As we shall now see, this calculation involves
consideration of yet another extended field configuration [6].
     Let us concentrate on the component ϕ of the scalar field multiplet that acquires an
expectation value ⟨ϕ⟩ in the true vacuum. For instance, in the theory of broken chiral
symmetry discussed in Section 19.5, ϕ would be the fourth component of a chiral four-vector.
It will turn out that, where barrier penetration is strongly suppressed, the other scalar fields
(including those of any Goldstone bosons) do not affect the dominant suppression factor in
the decay rate. For definiteness, we will take the Lagrangian density in the form
                                       1
                                  L = − ∂µ ϕ ∂ µ ϕ − V (ϕ).                            (23.8.1)
                                       2
We assume that the lowest-order effective potential V (ϕ) has a true minimum at ϕ = ⟨ϕ⟩
and a local minimum at ϕ = 0, and we adjust an additive constant in the Lagrangian

which the false vacuum state with scalar field expectation value zero will decay into the
true vacuum state with scalar field expectation value ⟨ϕ⟩.

Appendix A       Euclidean Path Integrals
This appendix will outline the use of Euclidean path integrals in quantum field theory.
As mentioned in Section 9.1, it is possible to formulate quantum field theory in a four-

Appendix B      A List of Homotopy Groups
This appendix presents a list of homotopy groups [40] for various manifolds. Here Z denotes
the group of the integers, with group composition defined by addition, so that zero is the
unit element. Also, Zn is the group of the integers modulo n. The trivial group, consisting
of the element 0, is denoted 0. Homotopy groups for direct products of manifolds may be
obtained from the homotopy groups of the manifolds themselves by the product rule:

                             πn (M1 × M2 ) = πn (M1 ) × πn (M2 ).

    Coset Spaces
       For any Lie group G and any Lie subgroup H ⊂ G,

                                 π2 (G/H) = ker{π1 (H) 7→ π1 (G)}.

    That is, π2 (G/H) is the subgroup of π1 (H) that maps into the trivial element of π1 (G)
    when H is embedded in G. As a special case,

                                π2 (G/H) = π1 (H)         for π1 (G) = 0.

        in four-dimensional Euclidean spacetime to make it possible to have topologically
        non-trivial field configurations at which the action is stationary?

        Suppose that enough higher derivative terms are added to the Lagrangian so that

        (Hint: Note that, as shown in Section 2.7, SU (2) is topologically the same as S3 .)

        winding number in an SU (4) gauge theory?

        small.

    Solutions to Weinberg Exercises
    These editorial solutions were added by Codex and are not part of Weinberg’s original text.

W.23.1. Let a configuration of characteristic size R be obtained by dilating a fixed configu-
        ration. In four Euclidean dimensions, a positive term containing k derivatives scales
        as
                                        Ik (R) = R4−k Ik (1).
         The usual two-derivative Goldstone action therefore scales as R2 and drives a non-
         trivial configuration to zero size. A four-derivative term is scale invariant, so it does
         not alter the derivative of the action with respect to R. To oppose collapse one needs
         a positive term that grows as R → 0, hence a term with more than four derivatives.
         The minimal possibility is a positive six-derivative invariant:

                                       I(R) = R2 I2 + R−2 I6 + · · · .

         It has a stationary scale R4 = I6 /I2 . Thus the required addition is a stabilizing higher-
         derivative interaction of order strictly greater than four (six derivatives at minimum),
         with a sign that makes its Euclidean contribution positive.

W.23.2. The vacuum manifold is
                                    SU (2)L × SU (2)R
                                                      ≃ SU (2) ≃ S 3 .
                                         SU (2)V

         Finite energy compactifies six-dimensional space to S 6 , so the sectors are labeled by

                                               π6 (S 3 ) = Z12 .

         Consequently the skyrmion charge is conserved only modulo 12. Charges add in Z12 :
         a skyrmion and an antiskyrmion cancel, and twelve unit skyrmions are topologically
         equivalent to the vacuum and may annihilate. This is a discrete Z12 conservation law
         rather than the integer-valued baryon-number law of the ordinary three-dimensional
         skyrmion.

W.23.3. Represent S n as the cube I n with its boundary collapsed to a base point, and let
        a, b, c, d be based maps I n → M. For n > 1, define two products: ∗1 concatenates
        maps in the first coordinate and ∗2 concatenates them in the second. The constant
        based map e is the identity for both products, up to based homotopy.




                                               – 564 –
          Subdividing the first two coordinates into four rectangles gives the interchange law

                                  (a ∗1 b) ∗2 (c ∗1 d) = (a ∗2 c) ∗1 (b ∗2 d).

          The two products first coincide:

                         a ∗1 b = (a ∗2 e) ∗1 (e ∗2 b) = (a ∗1 e) ∗2 (e ∗1 b) = a ∗2 b.

          Calling this common product simply ∗, a second use of the interchange law gives

                          a ∗ b = (e ∗1 a) ∗2 (b ∗1 e) = (e ∗2 b) ∗1 (a ∗2 e) = b ∗ a.

          Hence the group operation on πn (M) is commutative for every n > 1, so every higher
          homotopy group is Abelian.

S.23.1. Topology, Defect Codimension, and Causal Formation

       (a) Under the stated fixed boundary condition, all directions at |x| → ∞ represent
           the same chosen vacuum. Adjoining one point at infinity therefore gives the
           one-point compactification
                                         Rd ∪ {∞} ≃ S d ,
           and the configuration is a based map Φ : S d → M, with Φ(∞) the chosen
           vacuum. A continuous path through finite-energy nonsingular configurations is
           exactly a based homotopy, so it cannot change the class [Φ] ∈ πd (M).
           The class can change only if one of the hypotheses fails: the field may violate the
           fixed boundary data, leave the restricted space of maps into M, or become singu-
           lar. Each possibility exits the configuration space whose connected components
           are being classified. This is the origin of topological stability.
       (b) Take a small q-dimensional ball transverse to the defect. Its boundary links the
           core and is S q−1 . Away from the core the field lies in M, so its restriction to the
           linking sphere is a map
                                             S q−1 −→ M.
           The defect is topologically nontrivial precisely when this map is a nonzero ele-
           ment of πq−1 (M).
           In three dimensions the possibilities are
                                         defect    q classification
                                       domain wall 1    π0 (M)
                                         string    2    π1 (M)
                                        monopole 3 π2 (M).

           Two disconnected vacua have nontrivial π0 and permit walls. Since π1 (S 1 ) =
           Z, an S 1 vacuum permits strings. Since π2 (S 2 ) = Z, an S 2 vacuum permits
           monopoles. The other two entries in each of these simple examples are trivial.
        (c) Finite energy requires the two limits ϕ(+∞) and ϕ(−∞) independently to belong
            to {−v, +v}. A convenient orientation-sensitive charge is
                                              ϕ(+∞) − ϕ(−∞)

           the topologically trivial sector Q = 0. For the wall with Q = 1, complete the
           square:

(e) A correlation domain has volume of order ξ 3 . Neighboring domains may choose

    a core, trapping a defect.

    dimensions of walls, strings, and point defects.

S.23.7. Small-Instanton Convergence
       At fixed µ and g(µ), all factors except the power of ρ are constant, so
                                                                   11N
                                dn ∝ dρ ρb0 −5 ,        b0 − 5 =       − 5.
                                                                    3
       The integral at the lower endpoint converges when b0 − 5 > −1, or b0 > 4. For every
       N ≥ 2, b0 ≥ 22/3 > 4, and therefore
                              Z
                                dρ ρ11N/3−5 is ultraviolet convergent.
                                0


       The same one-loop expression grows as a positive power at large ρ, so its upper-end
       size integral does not converge. Large instantons probe the scale 1/ρ, where the run-
       ning gauge coupling becomes strong. Their action is no longer parametrically large,
       instantons cease to be dilute, and higher-loop and nonperturbative effects are unsup-
       pressed. The large-ρ behavior is therefore an infrared warning that the semiclassical
       formula has left its domain of validity, not a reliable quantitative prediction of an
       infinite density.

S.23.12. The Unique Negative Bounce Mode

       Differentiating the stated thin-wall action twice gives

                                    B ′′ (R) = 12π 2 σR − 6π 2 ϵR2 .

       At R∗ = 3σ/ϵ,
                                                       18π 2 σ 2
                                      B ′′ (R∗ ) = −             < 0.
                                                          ϵ
       The associated fluctuation expands or contracts the bubble, so this establishes a
       negative dilation direction in the thin-wall approximation. It does not by itself prove
       uniqueness. A separate spectral analysis of the full fluctuation operator establishes
       that, in this thin-wall regime, the bounce has exactly one negative eigenvalue.
       Steepest-descent integration through this mode produces a factor of i/2, giving an
       imaginary part to the metastable vacuum energy. By contrast, the four translational
       modes cost no action; integrating over the bounce center produces the total Euclidean
       spacetime volume, which becomes a decay rate per unit volume after division by that
       factor. The contour is fixed by analytic continuation from a stable potential, selecting
       the sign for which Γ/V = −2 Im Ef > 0.

        so every Bogomolny solution obeys the static Euler–Lagrange equation. With x re-

        zero-mechanical-energy trajectory joining two adjacent maxima of −V .
        If a third degenerate minimum lies between the endpoints, the first-order flow reaches
        it only at infinite x: near a nondegenerate minimum, d(ϕ − ϕ∗ )/dx is proportional
        to ϕ − ϕ∗ . A single smooth finite-width solution therefore cannot pass through it.
        The putative skipping configuration separates into two kinks with an arbitrarily long
        interval of the intermediate vacuum.

S.23.16. Gauge-Invariant Vortex Winding and Radial Gauge

        On a large circle a gauge transformation changes the scalar phase by α(R, ϑ). If
        eiα extends smoothly over the enclosed disk, its restriction to the boundary is null-
        homotopic. Equivalently,
                                          Z 2π
                                        1
                                               dϑ ∂ϑ α = 0.
                                       2π 0
        Hence it cannot change the winding n. A transformation with nonzero boundary
        winding would be singular or multivalued somewhere in the plane and is not an
        allowed smooth gauge transformation of the vortex.
        Define                                        Z r
                                       α(r, ϑ) = −q         ds Ar (s, ϑ).
                                                       0

        Then Ar 7→ Ar + q −1 ∂r α = 0. Smoothness of the original Cartesian gauge field at
        the origin makes this transformation regular there, and periodicity of Ar makes it
        single-valued in ϑ.
        By contrast, setting Aϑ to zero around a closed circle would require a periodic α
        satisfying                       I            I
                                                i   1
                                     0 = Ai dx +        dα.
                                                    q
        The second integral vanishes for a single-valued gauge transformation, whereas the
        first approaches the nonzero vortex flux 2πn/q. Thus nontrivial holonomy, equiva-
        lently nonzero flux, obstructs imposing Aϑ = 0 globally.

S.23.17. The Critical Abelian-Higgs Bogomolny Bound

        Covariant differentiation obeys the product rule because the gauge connections on ϕ
        and ϕ∗ cancel:
                                ∂i (ϕ∗ Dj ϕ) = (Di ϕ)∗ Dj ϕ + ϕ∗ Di Dj ϕ.




                                               – 588 –
    Direct expansion of Di = ∂i − iqAi also gives

                          [Di , Dj ]ϕ = −iq(∂i Aj − ∂j Ai )ϕ = −iqFij ϕ.

    Using
                       |D1 ϕ ± iD2 ϕ|2 = |Di ϕ|2 ∓ qB|ϕ|2 + divergence,
    the critical energy becomes
                      Z                                    
                                         1
                 E = d x |(D1 ± iD2 )ϕ| + {B ∓ q(v − |ϕ| )} ± qv 2 Φ.
                         2             2          2     2 2
                                         2

    Choosing the sign of the flux gives

                                     E ≥ qv 2 |Φ| = 2πv 2 |n|.

    Equality holds when

                          (D1 ± iD2 )ϕ = 0,         B = ±q(v 2 − |ϕ|2 ).

    Applying the opposite covariant derivative to the first equation and using [D1 , D2 ] =
    −iqB, together with the second equation, reproduces the scalar equation; differenti-
    ating the magnetic equation similarly gives Ampere’s equation. The bound is exactly
    linear in |n|, so a separated collection of unit vortices has the same energy as a co-
    incident n-vortex. The scalar attraction and magnetic repulsion cancel, yielding no
    static force at critical coupling.
